Specification-Driven Generation and Evaluation of Discrete-Event World Models via the DEVS Formalism

Zheyu Chen† Affiliation: †Zhili College, Tsinghua University    Zhuohuan Li‡ Affiliation: ‡Department of Industrial Engineering, Tsinghua University    Chuanhao Li‡ ††thanks: Corresponding Author Affiliation: {chenzhey22,lizhuohu23}@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn, chuanhao-li@tsinghua.edu.cn
Abstract

World models are essential for planning and evaluation in agentic systems, yet existing approaches lie at two extremes: hand-engineered simulators that offer consistency and reproducibility but are costly to adapt, and implicit neural models that are flexible but difficult to constrain, verify, and debug over long horizons. We seek a principled middle ground that combines the reliability of explicit simulators with the flexibility of learned models, allowing world models to be adapted during online execution. By targeting a broad class of environments whose dynamics are governed by the ordering, timing, and causality of discrete events, such as queueing and service operations, embodied task planning, and message-mediated multi-agent coordination, we advocate explicit, executable discrete-event world models synthesized directly from natural-language specifications. Our approach adopts the DEVS formalism and introduces a staged LLM-based generation pipeline that separates structural inference of component interactions from component-level event and timing logic. To evaluate generated models without a unique ground truth, simulators emit structured event traces that are validated against specification-derived temporal and semantic constraints, enabling reproducible verification and localized diagnostics. Together, these contributions produce world models that are consistent over long-horizon rollouts, verifiable from observable behavior, and efficient to synthesize on demand during online execution.

   

1 Introduction

As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as general-purpose agents, world models, i.e., models that support hypothetical rollouts of environment dynamics under candidate actions, have emerged as a central research focus. They are attractive for two reasons. First, agentic reinforcement learning increasingly relies on experience-driven scaling, which demands larger, more diverse, and more challenging environments; world models can help by generating simulated experience to improve learning efficiency [1, 2]. Second, LLM-based agents are expected to operate over extended time horizons, increasing the importance of long-horizon planning; world models enable agents to simulate and evaluate the consequences of candidate actions prior to execution, which reduces reliance on risky and costly online exploration [3, 4].

A growing body of work has explored world models across domains [5, 6], yet most existing approaches fall toward one of two ends of a spectrum. At one end are hand-engineered simulators that explicitly encode environment dynamics and support controlled experimentation [6]. Such simulators are typically reproducible and debuggable, but require substantial human effort and are often difficult or costly to adapt to new environments, particularly in online settings. At the other end are implicit approaches that prompt or train models to predict future states or observations conditioned on past events [3, 7]. While these methods offer greater flexibility and can be adapted online through prompting, they are often unreliable when used as long-horizon simulators: implicit dynamics are difficult to constrain or verify, small errors compound across multi-step rollouts, and assumptions about timing and causality remain latent, complicating failure diagnosis and targeted correction. As a result, a practically useful middle ground remains underdeveloped, namely, world models that are (i) consistent during long-horizon rollouts, (ii) reproducible and verifiable from observable behavior, and (iii) easy to modify or synthesize on demand during online execution.

In this paper, we argue that such a middle ground is attainable for an important class of environments whose dynamics are governed primarily by the ordering, timing, and causality of discrete interactions. Examples include network protocols and distributed systems, queueing and service operations, manufacturing and supply-chain workflows, embodied task planning [8], business process automation [9], and multi-agent coordination mediated by messages or events [10]. In these domains, environment evolution is naturally characterized as a sequence of timed discrete events, such as arrivals, departures, messages, failures, each inducing a state transition at a simulated time.

This motivates discrete-event world models, which capture environment dynamics as state transitions induced by discrete events and scheduled time advances, and explicitly surface event traces. They enforce structured state evolution and help maintain consistency over long-horizon rollouts, avoiding the unbounded drift common in implicit simulators. Treating event traces as first-class objects also makes timing and causality explicit, enabling reproducibility and verification from observable behavior, as well as fine-grained reasoning about alternative action sequences and long-horizon effects. Finally, by encoding dynamics through explicit events and state transition rules, discrete-event world models support online synthesis and on-demand adaptation.

To make this perspective operational, we formalize discrete-event world models as executable simulators synthesized directly from natural-language specifications provided by users or LLM agents, enabling construction and adaptation on demand. We introduce an LLM-based code-generation pipeline that translates a description of an environment composed of interacting components into an executable simulator that (i) exposes a standardized command-line interface for agent interventions and (ii) emits a structured event trace of the environment’s evolution, enabling reproducible execution and downstream analysis based on observable behavior.

This paradigm raises two key challenges. First, realistic environments can be structurally complex, comprising multiple interacting components with nontrivial timing and communication semantics. Directly synthesizing a monolithic simulator requires an LLM to infer system structure, interaction protocols, and component-level dynamics simultaneously; failures in any one part can invalidate the entire simulator. Second, natural-language specifications rarely determine a unique ground-truth implementation, so evaluation via code-level equivalence or stepwise prediction accuracy is ill-posed. Instead, evaluation should be specification-driven, asking whether executed behavior satisfies temporal and semantic constraints implied by the specification.

To address the first challenge, we adopt the Discrete Event System Specification (DEVS) formalism [11, 12] as the representation for world models. DEVS decomposes systems into interacting atomic and coupled components with explicit state, transition, and timing semantics. Leveraging this modularity, we introduce a staged generation pipeline in which the LLM first synthesizes the component hierarchy and interaction graph, and subsequently implements component-level behavioral logic. This decomposition enables parallel generation of atomic components, making rapid, on-demand synthesis feasible during online execution. Moreover, separating structural synthesis from component behavior improves efficiency and stability by isolating structural decisions from behavioral logic, reducing cross-component coupling, and increasing robustness to local generation errors.

To address the second challenge, we introduce a trace-based, specification-driven evaluation framework. Generated simulators are required to emit event traces conforming to a standardized schema that records event time, entity, type, and payload. Under controlled test scenarios, these traces are validated against rule sets encoding temporal relationships and semantic invariants derived from the specification, such as precedence and response constraints, timing bounds, and conservation or safety properties. When a violation occurs, the framework produces localized diagnostics identifying the violated constraint and the responsible entities and state variables, enabling systematic verification without reliance on a reference implementation.

Together, these design choices establish a specification-driven framework for generating, executing, and evaluating discrete-event world models from natural language. By combining DEVS-based modular synthesis with trace-level evaluation, our approach provides a scalable discrete-event foundation for long-horizon reasoning, producing executable artifacts with explicit interfaces and actionable diagnostic feedback to support systematic, iterative refinement. Beyond purely rule-based event and temporal dynamics, the proposed framework lays the foundation for generating hybrid discrete-event systems from natural-language specifications, including systems in which LLMs are embedded within DEVS components as event-generating or decision-making entities. This enables the synthesis of coordinated multi-agent systems for task solving, as well as LLM-driven simulations, such as social or organization simulations, specified and instantiated entirely through natural language.

2 Related Works

2.1 World Models: Explicit and Implicit Approaches

World models have long served as predictive mechanisms to support planning and reinforcement learning, enabling agents to reason about the consequences of actions before execution and to generate simulated experience for improved learning efficiency [1]. Broadly, existing work on world modeling can be categorized into two complementary approaches: explicit world models, in which environment dynamics are manually implemented inside executable simulators, and implicit world models, in which dynamics are captured by learned models, often neural networks.

Several works construct world models as human-designed, executable simulators with well-defined state representations and transition dynamics. For example, [13] utilize a robotic simulator as a world model and demonstrate that interaction with such a model can enhance the performance of language models on downstream tasks. Similarly, [6] present Web World Models, a carefully web-based simulator that captures the structure and dynamics of web environments to support controlled agent interaction and evaluation. These approaches emphasize executability, reproducibility, and precise control over environment dynamics. In parallel, recent work has explored whether environment dynamics can be modeled implicitly by large neural networks, particularly LLMs. In this paradigm, the world model is not represented as a standalone simulator; instead, environment dynamics are encoded in the model’s parameters and accessed through prediction during inference. LLMs are prompted or trained to predict future observations or outcomes conditioned on past events, and these predictions are used to guide action selection or planning [3, 4]. This approach has been applied across a range of domains, including web environments [4, 6, 14], video games and real-world video data [5], and robotic tasks involving visual, force, or other sensory feedback [15].

These two lines of work reflect different trade-offs in how world dynamics are represented and accessed. Explicit world models provide executable, transparent representations of environment dynamics but typically require substantial manual effort to design and adapt, while implicit neural world models offer greater flexibility and scalability by leveraging learned representations, at the cost of reduced explicitness and multi-turn consistency.

2.2 Symbolic and Programmatic World Model Generation

A closely related line of work focuses on generating structured representations of environment dynamics from natural language, with the goal of improving interpretability and enabling rule-based or formal verification. In the context of symbolic world or domain models, several approaches translate natural-language descriptions into executable planning representations such as PDDL, using plan execution behavior or task outcomes as evaluation signals [16, 17, 18]. Complementary efforts reduce reliance on expert supervision by incorporating environment interaction to iteratively refine generated planning domains [19].

Beyond planning-oriented representations, related work has explored generating system-level models from natural-language requirements in software and systems engineering. In particular, several studies synthesize SysML artifacts, such as structural diagrams or behavioral models, and evaluate them using consistency checks, requirement coverage, or simulation-based criteria [20, 21, 22]. These approaches emphasize requirements traceability, design validation, and alignment with established engineering workflows, but typically focus on static structure or high-level behavioral descriptions rather than executable environment dynamics.

Our work aligns with these efforts in seeking explicit, programmatic representations of environment dynamics from natural language, but differs in its choice of modeling formalism and evaluation focus. Compared to PDDL-based planning models, which emphasize symbolic state transitions and goal satisfaction in discrete steps, DEVS provides an execution-oriented semantics centered on discrete events, explicit time, and concurrent interactions, making it well suited for domains such as queues, workflows, distributed systems, and message-driven multi-agent settings. Relative to SysML-based approaches, which primarily support high-level system specification and design reasoning, DEVS offers precise simulation semantics and inherent executability, producing structured event traces that enable black-box, trace-based evaluation under controlled scenarios. Together, these properties position DEVS as a natural foundation for synthesizing and evaluating discrete-event world models from natural-language descriptions.

2.3 LLM-Based Code Generation and Long-Horizon Development

Recent research has extensively explored the capabilities of large language models and code agents for natural language driven software implementation, fixing issues in existing code repositories, and generating multi-file projects. Evaluations typically focus on unit-test-based functional correctness, issue-fixing success rates, or repository-level benchmarks. Examples include unit-test-driven functional correctness evaluation [23], repository-repair benchmarks based on real GitHub issues [24], and repository-level multi-file evaluation settings [25, 26].

The problem addressed in this paper likewise involves long-horizon code development: coordinating across multiple steps and files, and leveraging execution and tool feedback to iteratively advance the implementation. Existing work often summarizes complex processes with automatable, reproducible outcome metrics (e.g., test pass/fail or task completion rate) and evaluates systems on multi-step interactive software-engineering tasks or repository-level feature-implementation settings [27, 26, 28].

Our evaluation objectives differ fundamentally from these approaches. We require not only executable code but also conformance to a time-sensitive event-semantics specification, defined via standard-input interventions and a unified JSONL event format. Accordingly, our evaluation is closer to conformance testing, where correctness is judged by whether observable input/output behavior satisfies the specification, rather than by generic unit tests [29]. It also aligns with the runtime-verification perspective of checking specifications against execution traces [30].

2.4 Verification, Validation, and Conformance for Discrete-Event Models

Verification and validation (V&V) of discrete-event models and DEVS models have a long research history, including static consistency checks, simulation-based verification, and formal analysis of model composition. These approaches provide systematic tools for detecting specification violations. For instance, structural consistency verification can validate the structural definitions of coupled models prior to simulation [31]; behavioral-level verification is often instantiated as simulation-driven unit tests or semantic-consistency tests [32, 33]; and work that integrates DEVS with model checking and applies mixed V&V in hierarchical/multi-resolution compositional modeling illustrates a path that combines formal analysis with compositional verification [34, 35].

In line with this tradition, execution trajectories can serve as a direct basis for systematic evaluation: given input drivers and observation schemes, the runtime traces of the system under test can be compared against specified properties to determine whether the expected behavior is satisfied. This perspective is commonly framed as runtime verification (RV) in the broader software and systems verification literature, where specifications are checked online or offline against event/state sequences [30]. In discrete-event simulation, similar trace-based checking can be achieved by explicitly modeling properties and performing on-demand checks during simulation [36].

This paper similarly adopts trace-based system evaluation, but under a distinct context: the DEVS models are automatically synthesized by LLM-driven generators, resulting in highly diverse implementation forms. Consequently, the evaluation framework must center on interfaces and observable behaviors to accommodate diverse implementations, and provide actionable localization signals when specification violations are detected. Furthermore, evaluation should target property/behavioral conformance rather than relying on code-level equivalence to a single reference implementation. These requirements naturally connect to black-box testing frameworks and their diagnostic capabilities for failing cases [37]. They also echo metamorphic testing, which mitigates the oracle problem via metamorphic relations when reliable test oracles are unavailable [38].

3 Discrete-Event World Models and DEVS

In this section, we formalize discrete-event world models considered in this paper and introduce the DEVS formalism as the operational representation. Our goal is to precisely characterize (i) the notion of a discrete-event world, (ii) the input–output interface exposed by an executable world model, and (iii) its realization using DEVS, thereby establishing a rigorous foundation for the generation and evaluation methods developed in subsequent sections.

3.1 Problem Setup

We study the problem of constructing discrete-event world models from natural language descriptions. Such descriptions specify the entities involved in an environment, the types of discrete events that may occur, and temporal or causal relationships among events. In our framework, an discrete-event world model is realized as a simulator that instantiates a concrete interpretation of the described environment and serves as a predictive substrate for downstream tasks such as planning and evaluation. Figure 1 illustrates this through a warehouse robot fleet restocking task. The natural-language specification (top center) describes entities such as robots, chargers, and inventory, along with event types including order arrivals, task assignments, robot movements, charging events, and inventory updates. This description implicitly defines a world whose evolution is governed by discrete events rather than continuous dynamics.

Discrete-event world.

We define a discrete-event world as one in which the state changes only at isolated event times; between events, the state remains constant. In the warehouse example, the world state includes, for instance, the contents of the order queue, the locations and battery levels of robots, and inventory levels. State changes occur only when events such as an order arrival, a robot completing a task, or a charging operation finishing take place. Formally, a discrete-event world is represented as 𝒲=(ℰ,𝒮,Ω,𝒫,δ)\mathcal{W}=(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{S},\Omega,\mathcal{P},\delta), where ℰ\mathcal{E} is a finite set of entities, e.g., order queues, robots, chargers, inventory, 𝒮=∏e∈ℰ𝒮e\mathcal{S}=\prod_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{S}_{e} is the global state space with 𝒮e\mathcal{S}_{e} the local state space of entity ee, Ω\Omega is the event alphabet specifying event types, e.g., order arrival, task assignment, charge complete, and 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the payload space capturing event-specific data, e.g., order IDs, robot identifiers, SKUs.

The space of event instances is 𝒰:=Ω×𝒫\mathcal{U}:=\Omega\times\mathcal{P}, so that an individual event instance u=(ℓ,p)∈𝒰u=(\ell,p)\in\mathcal{U} corresponds, for example, to a specific order arrival or a particular robot completing a task. The transition relation δ:𝒮×𝒰×ℝ≥0→𝒮\delta:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{U}\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\rightarrow\mathcal{S} specifies the effect of applying an event instance and time advancement to the world state. This captures autonomous temporal processes, e.g., a robot completing a movement after a travel time, and interactions among entities, e.g., a dispatcher assigning a task to a robot.

Executable world models as simulators.

In our framework, an executable discrete-event world model is realized as an simulator, denoted as ℳ\mathcal{M}. It instantiates a concrete interpretation of the world 𝒲\mathcal{W}, operationalizes its event dynamics, and serves as a predictive substrate for downstream tasks as depicted on the left side of Figure 1.

The simulator is treated as a black-box executable with a fixed input–output interface. External interventions are drawn from a set 𝒜\mathcal{A} and provided as configuration arguments

ℐ=(a1,a2,…,am),ak∈𝒜,\mathcal{I}=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{m}),\qquad a_{k}\in\mathcal{A},

which parameterize execution at launch. In the warehouse example, these interventions include the number of robots, the choice of dispatching policy, the number of chargers, and the simulation horizon. Some tasks additionally provide an optional input stream 𝒥\mathcal{J} specifying exogenous inputs delivered during execution. We treat the overall external input to the simulator as the pair (ℐ,𝒥)(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}). Executing ℳ⁡(ℐ,𝒥)\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}) produces observable behavior in the form of an event trace 𝒯=(r1,r2,…)\mathcal{T}=(r_{1},r_{2},\ldots) with each trace record r∈𝒯r\in\mathcal{T} being a time-stamped output annotated with the emitting entity,

r=(t,e,ℓ,p)∈ℝ≥0×ℰ×Ω×𝒫.r=(t,e,\ell,p)\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times\mathcal{E}\times\Omega\times\mathcal{P}.

For example, this could correspond to an order arrival or a robot completing a charging operation at time tt.

3.2 DEVS as an Operational Representation

In this paper, we adopt Parallel DEVS as our representation formalism for ℳ\mathcal{M} [12]. Figure 1 (right) illustrates how the warehouse world is realized as a DEVS model. DEVS models 𝒲\mathcal{W} as a hierarchical composition of atomic models, which encapsulate local state and event-handling logic, and coupled models, which define how atomic or coupled models are composed and how events are routed among them. For example, robots, chargers, order queues, and inventory are each modeled as atomic models with well-defined timing and transition semantics. Interactions among entities, such as a dispatcher assigning tasks to robots or robots requesting charging, are realized through event passing in coupled models.

Formally, for each entity e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}, we define an atomic model

ℳe=(Xe,Ye,𝒮e,δinte,δexte,δcone,λe,tae),\mathcal{M}_{e}=\bigl(X_{e},Y_{e},\mathcal{S}_{e},\delta_{\mathrm{int}}^{e},\delta_{\mathrm{ext}}^{e},\delta_{\mathrm{con}}^{e},\lambda^{e},t_{a}^{e}\bigr),

where Xe,Ye⊆ΩX_{e},Y_{e}\subseteq\Omega are the admissible input and output event alphabets, 𝒮e\mathcal{S}_{e} is the local state space, δinte:𝒮e→𝒮e\delta_{\mathrm{int}}^{e}:\mathcal{S}_{e}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{e} is the internal transition function, δexte:𝒮e×ℝ≥0×ℬ⁡(Xe)→𝒮e\delta_{\mathrm{ext}}^{e}:\mathcal{S}_{e}\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times\mathcal{B}(X_{e})\rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{e} is the external transition function, with the real-valued argument denoting elapsed simulation time since last transition, δcone:𝒮e×ℬ⁡(Xe)→𝒮e\delta_{\mathrm{con}}^{e}:\mathcal{S}_{e}\times\mathcal{B}(X_{e})\rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{e} is the confluent transition function used when external input arrives exactly at an internal transition time, λe:𝒮e→ℬ⁡(Ye)\lambda^{e}:\mathcal{S}_{e}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}(Y_{e}) is the output function, and tae:𝒮e→ℝ≥0∪{∞}t_{a}^{e}:\mathcal{S}_{e}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\cup\{\infty\} is the time-advance function. Here ℬ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{B}(\cdot) denotes bags (multisets) of messages.

Operationally, an atomic model remains in state s∈𝒮es\in\mathcal{S}_{e} for tae​(s)t_{a}^{e}(s) units of simulated time; at that time it emits outputs via λe\lambda^{e} and performs an internal transition via δinte\delta_{\mathrm{int}}^{e}. If input arrives before the scheduled internal transition, the model applies δexte\delta_{\mathrm{ext}}^{e} using the elapsed time. If input arrives exactly at the internal transition time, δcone\delta_{\mathrm{con}}^{e} resolves the conflict.

Coupled models compose these atomic models and define how events are routed among them, yielding a hierarchical representation whose root corresponds to ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Formally, for any coupled model ℳc\mathcal{M}_{c} we write

ℳc=(Xc,Yc,𝒟c,{ℳd}d∈𝒟c,EICc,EOCc,ICc),\mathcal{M}_{c}=\bigl(X_{c},Y_{c},\mathcal{D}_{c},\{\mathcal{M}_{d}\}_{d\in\mathcal{D}_{c}},\mathrm{EIC}_{c},\mathrm{EOC}_{c},\mathrm{IC}_{c}\bigr),

where Xc,Yc∈ΩX_{c},Y_{c}\in\Omega are the admissible input and output event alphabets, 𝒟c\mathcal{D}_{c} is an index set of subcomponents and each ℳd\mathcal{M}_{d} is either atomic or coupled (recursively). The coupling specifications EICc\mathrm{EIC}_{c}, EOCc\mathrm{EOC}_{c}, and ICc\mathrm{IC}_{c} route bags of events from the external models into cc, from subcomponents of CC to the external models, and among subcomponents of ℳc\mathcal{M}_{c}, respectively. External inputs (ℐ,𝒥)(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}) to the simulator are injected through the root coupled model.

4 A DEVS-Based Model Generation Pipeline

Building on the DEVS formalization introduced in Section 3, we present a structured pipeline for generating a discrete-event simulator ℳ\mathcal{M} from natural-language environment specifications. The pipeline is designed specifically around the modular semantics of DEVS, using explicit component interfaces and coupling rules to guide synthesis.

The key idea is to exploit DEVS modularity to decompose model generation into a collection of well-scoped, contract-driven sub-tasks assigned to specialized LLM agents. Each component is generated against a fixed interface contract defined by a rigorous JSON schema (see App. A), which is established during an initial structural synthesis stage. These interfaces serve as contracts that constrain subsequent component-level generation, allowing each atomic model to be synthesized independently using only local context, while remaining globally consistent with the system architecture.

This DEVS-specific decomposition decouples the complexity of code generation from the scale of the environment: increasing the number of components does not increase the contextual burden of generating any single component. As a result, the pipeline supports scalable, reliable synthesis of complex discrete-event models directly from natural language. Figure 2 illustrates the overall procedure using the warehouse robot fleet restocking example.

4.1 Overview of the Generation Pipeline

The generation pipeline takes as input (i) a natural-language environment specification SS describing entities, events, and timing or causal constraints, and (ii) a contract CC that fixes the external interface (ℐ,𝒥)(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}) and trace schema 𝒯\mathcal{T}. (See App. D.1 for the complete textual specification and contract used in a real data example ABP). The output is a simulator ℳ\mathcal{M} implementing a DEVS model, with a trace logger that emits JSONL records conforming to 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Algorithm 1 formalizes the pipeline consisting of two stages: (1)Structural synthesis Infer the model hierarchy, port schemas, and interaction graph from SS and CC, and summarize them as a structured PlanTree. Detailed see Alg. 2. (2)Behavioral synthesis Implement atomic models with explicit state-transition and timing behavior based on the PlanTree, and compose them into a hierarchical coupled model with an execution interface and trace logger. Detail see Alg. 3. Although executed sequentially, they are not rigidly isolated: structural synthesis fixes interfaces and coupling patterns, providing architectural blueprint that constrains and enables concurrent behavioral synthesis of individual components.

4.2 Structural Synthesis Stage

This stage determines the architectural scaffold of the simulator, i.e., which components exist, how they are composed, and how they exchange events. Each component corresponds to a conceptual entity in the environment (e.g., robots, stations, queues, chargers), and interactions correspond to discrete events exchanged through explicit ports. Structural synthesis yields a single architectural artifact comprising (i) a component hierarchy with assigned model types (atomic or coupled), (ii) per-component input/output port schemas and behavioral logic specifications, and (iii) an interaction graph specifying routed event types. This artifact is represented as a typed tree, PlanTree, augmented with explicit coupling edges. Figure 2 visualizes the artifact produced by this stage for the warehouse robot fleet restocking example. We also provide a visual representation of the generated PlanTree for the example ABP in App. D.2, which details the decomposed hierarchy and interface schemas.

Prompting and Validation.

Structural synthesis is carried out by three specialized LLM agents utilizing the prompts defined in App. B.1: (i) A Classifier determines whether a component should be atomic or coupled based on functional complexity; (ii) A Splitter decomposes coupled models into child components and defines their interaction graph (the coupling); (iii) A Formulator translates atomic requirements into strict ModelSpecification JSON objects (see App. A), separating logic description from interface definition. Instead of rigidly enforcing every interface detail top-down, this stage focuses on establishing the system topology. While it proposes an initial interface schema to guide generation, the final interface contract is resolved dynamically during the implementation phase.

4.3 Behavioral Synthesis Stage

Following the structural planning, the framework constructs the simulator through a bottom-up, parallelized process. This stage encompasses both the synthesis of atomic behavioral logic and the adaptive assembly of coupled models.

Parallel Synthesis of Atomic Models.

Each atomic model maintains explicit internal state and defines how that state evolves under (i) incoming messages, (ii) internally scheduled events, and (iii) elapsed time. Timing behavior, such as processing delays, periodic actions, timeouts, or stochastic service times, is encoded directly in the time-advance function and the internal transition logic.

Component synthesis is performed independently by the Model Creator agent (App B). The agent is conditioned on the ModelSpecification from the structural stage and a set of injected Global Engineering Standards(App. B) that enforce type safety and library constraints. The resulting artifacts include per-component state definitions, event handlers, and timing rules. This bottom-up approach limits the scope of each generation task and promotes interface consistency. Its independence also allows us to maximize parallelization, significantly reducing generation time for large-scale environments. We provide a visualization of the generated model in App. D.3.

Adaptive Coupling via Interface Summarization.

To address potential semantic drifts where the generated code of a component might slightly deviate from the initial structural plan, we introduce an adaptive assembly step. Once a set of sibling components is implemented, a Summarizer agent analyzes their source code to extract the “ground-truth” interfaces (see App. B). The generation of their parent coupled model is then conditioned on these summaries rather than the original plan. This ensures that the coupling logic (i.e., how components are wired together) adapts to the actual implementation of the sub-components, preventing integration failures caused by minor interface mismatches. This recursive process continues upward until the root coupled model is synthesized.

Executable Simulator Interface.

Once components are synthesized, they are assembled into a DEVS simulator that implements the execution contract in Section 3. The assembled simulator parses configuration arguments ℐ\mathcal{I} (and optional input stream 𝒥\mathcal{J}), initializes component parameters and state, and emits a structured JSONL event trace during execution. The root coupled model exposes a minimal external interface: inputs correspond to exogenous events and outputs correspond to trace records. This design enables black-box execution and trace-based evaluation independent of internal implementation choices.

Concretely, ℐ\mathcal{I} parameterizes the simulator at launch (e.g., rates, capacities, horizons), while 𝒥\mathcal{J} is parsed by an input adapter into exogenous events that are injected at the root input port during execution. When no input stream is provided, 𝒥\mathcal{J} is empty and the simulator evolves solely from its initialized state and internal scheduling.

5 Trace-Based Evaluation of World Models

To rigorously assess whether a simulator ℳ\mathcal{M} generated by Algorithm 1 conforms to a natural-language specification SS, we introduce an evaluation benchmark grounded in trace-based conformance. Unlike conventional code generation benchmarks that assess correctness via functional input–output equivalence, our setting requires validating simulated execution trajectories. Specifically, evaluation focuses on whether emitted event traces satisfy temporal, causal, and semantic constraints implied by specification.

5.1 Trace-Based Evaluation Criteria

We evaluate generated world models using criteria defined over their emitted event traces. Rather than comparing code directly, our evaluation checks whether the observable behavior of ℳ\mathcal{M} conforms to constraints implied by the natural-language specification SS. This also serves as the basis for our dataset construction and evaluation procedure.

Operational success.

We first require that a generated simulator ℳ\mathcal{M} is usable as a software artifact. (1)Executable: The simulator must compile and run successfully inside a standard Docker environment. (2)Observable: The simulator must adhere to the I/O contract and event trace schema specified in CC, emitting event traces in the prescribed JSONL format (timestamp, entity, event type) to enable automated parsing and analysis.

Behavioral conformance.

For simulators ℳ\mathcal{M} that satisfy the operational criteria, we evaluate behavioral correctness by checking trace-level constraints derived from the specification SS. We manually implement these constraints based on the semantics of each task. They operate at two levels:

  • •

    Component-level: Constraints on the internal evolution of individual components, such as whether state transitions and timing behavior are consistent with the specification, e.g., correct waiting-time computation in a queue.

  • •

    System-level: Constraints on causal and temporal relationships across interacting components. These detect common failure modes in LLM-generated simulators, including events occurring between components that are not coupled and effects appearing before their causes.

5.2 Dataset Construction and Composition

We construct a curated dataset designed to probe specific world modeling capabilities. Our construction methodology prioritizes the authenticity of the simulation logic and the diversity of the modeling challenges.

To avoid the pitfalls of synthetic or trivial toy problems, we employ a reverse-engineering strategy. We select high-quality, open-source DEVS models, e.g., network protocols, industrial supply chains, and extract their core dynamics. These are rewritten into natural language specifications, while the original code is instrumented to harvest ground-truth event traces, ensuring every behavioral rule in our verification oracle is grounded in a working, realistic system.

Data assets.

Each benchmark scenario is a self-contained evaluation package containing:

  • •

    Specification: Natural language description of entities, state logic, and interaction rules of the environment.

  • •

    I/O contract: Strict definitions for intervention arguments and the output event schema.

  • •

    Test suite: A set of standard inputs (ℐ\mathcal{I}) designed to stress-test specific causal dependencies.

  • •

    Verification oracle: Executable checkers implementing the behavioral criteria in Section 5.1, validating traces against domain-specific constraints, e.g., verifying that packet latency obeys physical link properties.

Input granularity and quality.

The natural-language specifications are standardized to function as functional requirements. They are designed to be (1) implementation-agnostic, i.e., they describe what the system does without prescribing how it should be implemented, avoiding references to DEVS constructs, port names, or code structure; (2) behaviorally precise, i.e., while abstracting away implementation details, they provide unambiguous information about timing logic and causal relationships, minimizing the need for the model to invent domain rules.

Dataset composition.

We design a canonical set of scenarios that span orthogonal dimensions of difficulty. As summarized in Table 1, the benchmark is stratified along two axes. First, in terms of domain semantics, the scenarios cover three broad classes: service operations, network protocols, and physical dynamics. Second, in terms of dynamic features, they capture a range of discrete-event behaviors, including stochastic queuing, schedule-driven delays, continuous dynamics via ODE approximations, and complex nested state machines. More details about these scenarios and their specifications are provided in App. C.

5.3 Metrics and Experimental Protocol

To assess the quality of a simulator ℳ\mathcal{M} generated for a given benchmark scenario, we define a Test Suite 𝒟={d1,d2,…,dm}\mathcal{D}=\{d_{1},d_{2},\dots,d_{m}\} consisting of mm distinct data points with varying difficulty levels, e.g., from smoke tests to heavy-load scenarios. Each data points corresponds to one specific choice of (ℐ,𝒥)(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}) defined in Section 3.

For each generated simulator, we calculate two aggregated scores based on its performance across this test suite.

Operational success score (OSS).

This measures the robustness and executability coverage of the simulator. For each data point di∈𝒟d_{i}\in\mathcal{D}, we define a validity indicator viv_{i}:

vi=𝕀⁡(ExitCode=0)⋅𝕀⁡(NoTimeout)⋅𝕀⁡(ValidLog)v_{i}=\mathbb{I}(\text{ExitCode}=0)\cdot\mathbb{I}(\text{NoTimeout})\cdot\mathbb{I}(\text{ValidLog}) (1)

The simulator achieves a validity score of 1 only if it executes without crashing and adheres to the I/O contract for that specific input. We use SO​S​S=1m​∑i=1mviS_{OSS}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_{i} to denote the success rate across the entire test suite 𝒟\mathcal{D}, which penalizes brittle models that may function on simple inputs but crash under complex loads.

Behavioral conformance score (BCS).

For data points did_{i} on which the simulator executes successfully (vi=1v_{i}=1), we assess its simulation fidelity. To ensure balanced assessment, we employ a Macro-Average strategy that weights component logic and system consistency equally. Let ℛcomp\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{comp}} be the set of component-level rules and ℛsys\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sys}} be the set of system-level rules introduced in Section 5.1. Note that for stochastic scenarios, ℛsys\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sys}} inherently includes statistical distribution checks to verify probabilistic dynamics.

The conformance score cic_{i} for a data point did_{i} is defined as:

ci=12​vi​(∑r∈ℛcomp𝕀⁡(r⁡(𝒯i))|ℛcomp|⏟Local Logic+∑r∈ℛsys𝕀⁡(r⁡(𝒯i))|ℛsys|⏟Global Consistency)c_{i}=\frac{1}{2}v_{i}\left(\underbrace{\frac{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{comp}}}\mathbb{I}(r(\mathcal{T}_{i}))}{|\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{comp}}|}}_{\text{Local Logic}}+\underbrace{\frac{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sys}}}\mathbb{I}(r(\mathcal{T}_{i}))}{|\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sys}}|}}_{\text{Global Consistency}}\right) (2)

where 𝒯i=ℳ⁡(di)\mathcal{T}_{i}=\mathcal{M}(d_{i}) is the event trace generated by the simulator ℳ\mathcal{M} with input did_{i}. We use SB​C​S=1m​∑i=1mciS_{BCS}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_{i} to denote the average conformance over the test suite 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

6 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate the proposed generation pipeline described in Algorithm 1, henceforth referred to as DEVS-Gen, against state-of-the-art LLM-based software engineering agents. Our experiments are designed to answer three key questions: (i) Effectiveness: Can DEVS-Gen synthesize correct and executable world models across diverse domains? (ii) Efficiency: How does the cost (time and tokens) of DEVS-Gen compare to iterative agentic baselines? (iii) Scalability: Does the modular design of DEVS enable efficient parallel synthesis for larger systems?

6.1 Experimental Setup

We conduct experiments using the 7 scenarios listed in Table 1, which vary in scale, dynamic characteristics (e.g., ODE-based vs. logic-based), and interaction complexity.

We compare DEVS-Gen against two widely used open-source software engineering agents, OpenHands [39] and SWE-Agent [27]. To isolate the impact of structured generation from iterative debugging, we evaluate two variants of each baseline, including (i) Standard (Iterative): Default configurations of OpenHands with Terminal, FileEditor, and TaskTracker tools and SWE-Agent using a Python 3.11 environment with Simpy and xdevs.py. These agents may execute code, inspect logs, and self-correct. (ii) Lite (Non-Iterative): OpenHands-Lite and SWE-Agent-Lite, which are restricted in interaction turns and lack execution tools. This setting approximates a single-pass generation regime comparable to DEVS-Gen, enabling a controlled comparison between structured generation and iterative debugging.

All methods are evaluated across various LLM backbones. The Large model sets include GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Pro, GLM-4.7, and Claude-3.5-Sonnet, while the Small model sets include Llama-4-17B, GLM-4.7-Flash, Gemini-3-Flash, and Qwen3-Coder-30B. We report SO​S​SS_{OSS} and SB​C​SS_{BCS} as defined in Section 5.3. Efficiency is measured using wall-clock time (seconds) and token consumption. Runs that exceed a strict timeout are assigned zero scores, a time cost of 10410^{4}, and a token cost of 10710^{7}.

6.2 Results on Effectiveness

The operational success score SO​S​SS_{OSS} and behavioral conformance score SB​C​SS_{BCS} across all models and frameworks are reported in Table 2 (averaged over 33 independent runs).

Despite lacking the ability to execute code and self-correct, DEVS-Gen achieves competitive SO​S​SS_{OSS} and SB​C​SS_{BCS} scores compared to the fully agentic baselines. For instance, with GPT-5.2, DEVS-Gen achieves an SO​S​SS_{OSS} of 0.86, closely trailing the iterative OpenHands (0.96) and outperforming SWE-Agent (0.89). This suggests that the structured decomposition provided by the DEVS formalism effectively acts as a “correct-by-construction" guide, reducing the reliance on trial-and-error loops.

The importance of this structure becomes evident when comparing DEVS-Gen to the Lite baselines. When constrained to a comparable non-iterative compute budget, baseline performance degrades substantially. For example, under GLM-4.7, OpenHands-Lite’s SO​S​SS_{OSS} drops to 0.48 and SWE-Agent-Lite drops to 0.44, whereas DEVS-Gen maintains 0.87. This indicates that baseline agents rely heavily on the verify-fix loop to resolve errors, whereas DEVS-Gen’s contract-based generation yields functional code in one pass.

On smaller models (e.g., GLM-4.7-Flash, Gemini 3 Flash), DEVS-Gen demonstrates superior stability. While SWE-Agent frequently fails to produce executable code (SO​S​SS_{OSS} 0.13 for GLM-4.7-Flash), DEVS-Gen achieves an SO​S​SS_{OSS} of 0.48. This resilience is attributed to the modular generation pipeline, which breaks the complex simulation task into smaller, locally scoped sub-problems that are manageable for weaker models.

6.3 Results on Efficiency

Efficiency.

A critical advantage of DEVS-Gen over baseline agents is its predictable resource consumption. While agentic frameworks, e.g., SWE-Agent, rely on potentially unbounded debugging loops, incurring high latency and token costs when the model struggles, DEVS-Gen follows a structured, forward-pass synthesis process. Table 3 compares the average wall-clock time and token consumption (measured in log10\log_{10} tokens) across the two model sets.

As shown in Table 3, DEVS-Gen achieves a substantial reduction in token costs. On large models, it reduces consumption by approximately 0.80.8 orders of magnitude compared to SWE-Agent (equivalent to a ∼6×\sim 6\times reduction in raw tokens). This gap widens on small models, where DEVS-Gen uses over 10×10\times fewer tokens than OpenHands (log10\log_{10} 5.19 vs 6.25). This efficiency stems from our architecture: instead of paying for the entire context history of a prolonged debugging session, DEVS-Gen only consumes tokens for the structural plan and local component generation.

The time advantage is equally pronounced, particularly for smaller models. Weak models (e.g., Llama-4-17b) often cause standard agents to enter stagnation loops, running until timeout caps are reached (averaging >5000>5000s). In contrast, DEVS-Gen fails fast or succeeds linearly, keeping the average runtime around 1575s. Even on capable large models, DEVS-Gen remains competitive with the highly optimized OpenHands runtime while maintaining superior token economy.

6.4 Results on Scalability

A key architectural advantage of DEVS-Gen is its ability to decouple the synthesis process, which permits the parallel execution of structural planning and atomic model implementation. Predicated on the standard modeling practice where a coupled model aggregates at least two subcomponents, the depth of the system hierarchy grows logarithmically with the total number of components NN. Consequently, the theoretical synthesis latency is governed by the critical path of this hierarchy rather than the sequential accumulation of all tasks. This structural property reduces the time complexity from linear O⁡(N)O(N) (characteristic of serial approaches), to logarithmic O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N).

To validate this, we conducted an ablation study using GPT-5.2 on the DEVS-Gen framework, comparing the wall-clock time of Serial execution versus Parallel execution. As shown in Figure 3, we analyze the speed-up across the two phases:

  • •

    Planning Phase: Theoretically, the recursive planning algorithm allows independent branches of the system hierarchy to be decomposed concurrently. However, as observed in Figure 3, the empirical speedup is modest. This is primarily due to the scale of our current benchmark scenarios: the system hierarchies are relatively shallow, meaning the overhead of network requests and thread management outweighs the benefits of parallelizing the lightweight component classification tasks. We expect this speedup to become significant only in much larger, deeply nested systems.

  • •

    Generation Phase: The acceleration is substantial, achieving a ∼4.7×\sim 4.7\times speedup. Since atomic models (leaf nodes) encapsulate the bulk of the complex logic (state transitions and logic implementation), their generation is the computational bottleneck. Our framework successfully isolates these tasks, allowing them to be synthesized simultaneously.

This result proves the scalability of DEVS-Gen. While standard agentic loops face super-linear growth in time and context costs as system complexity increases, our modular approach ensures that the synthesis time grows logarithmically, making it feasible for large-scale world modeling.

Appendix A Structured Intermediate Representations

The ModelSpecification class serves as the central definition for any DEVS component. It strictly separates the functional logic from the logging requirements and enforces precise typing for input and output ports via PortEntity and ProtocolSpec.

Appendix B Agent Prompt Templates

This section presents the core prompt templates used in our generation pipeline. Each prompt is designed using a "Role-Task-Constraint" structure, injecting the structured context data defined in Appendix A.

B.1 Architectural Planning Agents

The Model Spec Formulator is responsible for translating vague natural language requirements into the strict ModelSpecification schema. It is explicitly instructed to separate core logic from external control artifacts.

⬇
1
2 ## [Role \& Objective]
3 You are a **DEVS Logic Architect**. Your task is to analyze the requirements and produce a strict specification for the core model ‘{name}‘.
4
5 **Your Goal**:
6 1. **Separate Concerns**: Isolate the *Core Logic* (Model) from the *External Controller*.
7 - The External Controller is responsible for stdin reading, external event injecting, arguments parsing, simulation control, and writing list[dict] logs in logger to stdout/stderr as JSONL.
8 - The Core Model is responsible for the internal logic, state, and writing logs to logger.
9 2. **Extract Logic**: You are not writing code, but you MUST extract the specific algorithmic rules (model structure, math, probabilities, delays) into the ‘function‘ field.
10 3. **Extract Logging**: If any logging/event_output is required, describe what to log in the ‘logging‘ field.
11 - You can add new logging events, but do not change the existing ones.
12 - Unless specified, the output should be completed by the core model.
13
14 ## [Input Data]
15 **Target Model Name**: ‘{name}‘
16 **Raw Requirements**:
17 {req}
18
19 **System Context (Environment)**:
20 {context_str}
21
22 **Reviewer Feedback**:
23 {feedback}

25 ## [Field Filling Guidelines (CRITICAL)]
26
27 You MUST follow these strict rules when populating the JSON fields:
28
29 ### ‘core_model.function‘ (The Logic Source of Truth)
30 * **Rule**: You **MUST COPY \& TRANSLATE** specific business rules from the Raw Requirements into bullet points.
31 * State: "Maintain a balance variable."
32 * Math: "Update: balance = balance - amount."
33 * Probability: "Logic: 50% chance to pass, 50% to fail."
34 * Timing: "Delay: Processing takes exactly 10.0 seconds."
35 * Anything else.
36 * **Ambiguity**: If requirements conflict, choose the most specific one.
37
38 ### ‘core_model.logging‘:
39 * If the raw requirements specify the output, it should be implemented through logging. Describe them in the ‘logging‘ field. Do not create external output ports for writing ‘stdout‘.
40 - Special: If the output format (key, event, etc. ) is specified, you must clearly state them, because the output checker will directly parse the logs.
41 - Special: If you are expected to output something at the end of the simulation, you can say it should log at the ‘exit‘ method.
42
43 ### ‘core_model.input_ports‘ / ‘output_ports‘ -> ‘structure‘
44 * **Rule**: If ‘type‘ is ‘dict‘ or ‘list‘, the ‘structure‘ field **CANNOT be vague**.
45 * **Format**: Use Python-like pseudo-code to define keys and types.
46 * *Rejectable*: ‘structure="User object"‘
47 * *Acceptable*: ‘structure="{{’id’: int, ’amount’: float, ’valid’: bool}}"‘
48
49 ### ‘core_model.input_ports‘ / ‘output_ports‘ -> ‘protocol‘
50 * **‘initial_state‘**: Usually "None" for standard event ports. If it’s a credit-based system, specify initial credits.
51 * **‘initial_signal‘**: Usually "None". Only specify if the model MUST send a message at t=0.
52
53 ### ‘controller_info‘ (The External Logic Container)
54 * **Rule**: Put **ALL** implementation details related to the Simulation Engine or OS here.
55 * **Content**:
56 * "Reading from sys.stdin and parsing lines (If any)."
57 * "Inject the input data into the core model (if any). "
58 * "Parse the arguments and control the simulation to run for a specific simulation time."
59 * "Parsing command line arguments (argparse)."
60 * "Writing logs from logger to stdout/stderr."
61 * The random seed setting is recommended to be set here.
62 * **Reason**: Keeping this out of ‘core_model‘ prevents the checker from rejecting your design for "Engine Violation".
63
64 ## [Design Constraints]
65 - **Time Unit**: You must specify the time unit in the ‘function‘ field (e.g., "1 unit = 1 second" or "1 unit is 10 millisecond").
66 - **Logging**: The model uses an internal logger for output. Do NOT create output ports for logs.

The Coupled Splitter decomposes a high-level model into its immediate children. It includes specific instructions to prevent "Gold Plating" (over-design) and to detect potential cold-start deadlocks in feedback loops.

⬇
1 ## [Task]
2 You are a DEVS System Architect. The model ‘{name}‘ has been identified as a **COUPLED** model.
3 Your task is to decompose it into its **DIRECT** children (Sub-models).
4
5 **Utils Provided to DEVS Models**:
6 - Logger: we implemented a customized logger to collect log messages in a standard way.
7 - get_current_time: we implemented a function to get the current simulation time.
8
9 ## [Architecture Strategy]
10 Before generating fields, adhere to these structural rules:
11 - **Hierarchical Granularity**: Decompose only to the **immediate next level**, and seperate to several meaningful children. Do NOT jump to bottom-level atomic components if an intermediate grouping makes sense. e.g. Hospital -> Departments -> Doctors.
12 - You should always decompose a coupled model into **at least** two children.
13 - Multiplicity \& Instantiation:
14 - Rule: The children_plan list defines CLASSES (Types), not instances. You must define a Class EXACTLY ONCE, even if it is used multiple times.
15 - Instance Names: The coupling_specification determines the Instance Names.
16 - Scenario A (Loops): If you need 5 Servers, define ONE child Server. In coupling, say "Instantiate 5 Servers as server_0 to server_4".
17 - Scenario B (Discrete Roles): If you need a "Forward Channel" and a "Backward Channel" with identical logic, define ONE child Channel. In coupling, say "Instantiate Channel as fwd_ch and bwd_ch".
18 - Wiring: Always use Instance Names (e.g., server_0, fwd_ch) in your wiring descriptions, NOT the Class Name.
19 - **Child or Sibling**: Identify if a sub-model should be another one’s child or a sibling. If A mainly interacts with the components of B, then A should be B’s child, do not make A a sibling of B.
20 - Provide a clear class name for each child (a valid Python identifier).
21 - Pass-through Principle: You are a structural architect, not a behavior designer. Your job is to move the existing logic requirements from the Parent to the correct Children, not to create new logic.
22
23 ## [Field Generation Guidelines]
24 You must generate a ‘children_plan‘ where each child contains the following specific fields. Follow these constraints strictly:
25
26 ### 1. function (Logic Delegation \& Fidelity)
27 Defines the responsibility boundaries based strictly on the Parent Spec.
28 - Scope Assignment: Identify which part of the [Parent Model Specification]’s logic is delegated to this child.
29 - Intelligent Strict Fidelity (Copy Rule): You must copy most of the Parent Spec’s constraints (e.g. "Service time = Exp(5)"), especially the calculation, coupling, units. Meanwhile, you should adapt implementation details if they are logically incomplete.
30 - You are only allowed to enrich the flow between childs, and make sure the external interface are exactly the same.
31 - **Example**: If the Spec implies tracking a specific ‘customer_id‘ for logging, but defines all ports as simple strings:
32 - The **Internal Port** between ‘Child_A‘ and ‘Child_B‘ SHOULD be upgraded to a ‘dict‘ (e.g., ‘{{’signal’: ’next’, ’id’: 123}}‘).
33 - The **External Output Port** (if the signal leaves the system) MUST remain a ‘str‘ (implying ‘Child_B‘ must strip the metadata before sending to the parent’s output).
34 - No Over-Design (Stop Rule): If the [Parent Model Specification] is vague about a detail (e.g., it just says "Process the request" without specifying how), DO NOT invent a mechanism (e.g., do NOT write "Process using FIFO queue" if FIFO wasn’t mentioned). Leave undefined details for the next level of decomposition.
35 - Black Box View: Describe the input-to-output behavior. Do not mention internal sub-components (grand-children) or how they are wired inside this child unless it is explicitly mentioned in the Parent Spec.
36
37 ### 2. logging
38 - **Inheritance**: extract the logging information from [Parent Model Specification] and assign every entry to one or more specific child responsible for that entry. Strictly keep the logging format (including field names, event names, and entity names) consistent with the Parent Spec.
39 - Describe the logging format in the field ‘logging‘ of every child seperatedly, especially the standardized fields and values. Must keep the same format as the Parent Spec (You must specify the field names, etc. in the logging field of the child, because it could not see the parent’s logging field).
40 - If the parent’s logging state the key names of the logging, you must copy the (1)key names, (2)event names, (3)value format, (4)etc., into the corresponding child’s logging field.
41
42 ### 3. input_ports / output_ports
43 *Defines the interface. Includes Port Encapsulation and Data Schema.*
44 - **Encapsulation**: Explicitly declare ALL ports. Even if the child is a Coupled model, it needs physical ports to act as a gateway for its internal logic.
45 - **Coupling Logic**: all the ports found in [Parent Model Specification] must be assigned to one or more specific child responsible for that task. And the internal coupling logic should also be clear.
46 - Definition: Describe the wiring using Instance Names.
47 - Every parent input_port should be connected to one or more child input_ports.
48 - Every parent output_port should be connected with one or more child output_ports.
49 - **Multiplicity Handling**: If connecting to a Multiplicity Child (e.g. 5 Servers), usage of Index Placeholders (e.g., ‘server_{{i}}‘) in the coupling description is encouraged to denote the pattern.
50 - **Completness**: The couplings between the children should be complete for their own internal logic.
51 - **Multiplicity**: If multiple identical ports exist for one child(e.g., Router has 5 ports connecting to 5 Servers), define the port **ONCE**, and state their instance names clearly using placeholders (e.g., name: "packet_{{i}}_out")
52 - ‘structure‘: Follow the Data Type Strictness.
53 - ‘protocol‘: how the child interacts with its neighbors (Parent/Siblings). This aggregates the Context, Protocol, and Handshake logic. And you should make sure the target port do exists.
54 - **Context Awareness**: Explicitly name the partner (instance name), and the target port in interactions. And you MUST explicitly check the partner’s role to prevent mismatches. e.g. "Receives processed frame from [Sibling-Decoder: prossed_frame] or raw data from [Parent: raw_data]." (Discribe the partner from the child’s perspective)
55 - For EIC and EOC, just extract the ports from the [Parent Model Specification] and assign them to the specific child responsible for that port.
56 - For IC: ensure its I/O ports and External Protocol match perfectly with its **siblings** (the other children you are creating), and explain the following:
57 - **Initial State**: Describe port state at T=0 (e.g., "empty", "waiting", "has initial token").
58 - **Initial Signals**: If port sends signals at startup, describe them (e.g., "Sends 5 ’ready’ signals to [Sibling-Manager: task_in] at T=0").
59 - **Flow Description**: Briefly explain data/signal flow and any constraints.
60
61 ### 4. model_init_args
62 *Defines the configuration parameters.*
63 - **Inheritance**: Map the numerical/logical parameters found in [Parent Model Specification] to these arguments (e.g., pass ‘queue_capacity=100‘ if the parent spec says so).
64 - Follow the Data Type Strictness.
65 - Ensure it include a field ‘name: str‘, which is the unique name of the model instance.
66
67 ### Data Type Strictness
68 1. **Type Descriptions**:
69 - This is the requirements for the ‘model_init_args‘, ‘input_ports‘, and ‘output_ports‘.
70 - Only int, float, bool, str, dict, list are allowed.
71 2. **Complex Type Schema**:
72 - For any input or output port that uses a ’dict’ or ’list’ type, you MUST explicitly describe the structure in the structure field. This includes listing all keys, their types, and a brief structure for each key.
73 - **No Gold Plating**: strictly adhere to the data fields specified in the [Parent Model Specification] and [System Context]. **DO NOT** add optional fields (like ‘currency‘, ‘timestamp‘, ‘trace_id‘) unless they are explicitly mentioned. Keep the data schema minimal and functional.
74 - *Exception*: If the parent model specification does not specify the data structure, you should implement it.
75 - Example: type="dict", structure="Job info containing keys: ’id’ (int): the job id , ’arrival_time’ (float): the arrival time of the job , and ’priority’ (int): the priority of the job, 0 for top, bigger implies lower priotiry."
76
77 ### Prevent Cold-Start Deadlocks
78 **Check for Circular Dependencies**: If there’s a closed loop (e.g. (1)Manager send job to Worker after receiving finished job from Worker, (2) A→B→C→A, (3) Queue -> Router -> Processor), you should prevent the cold-start deadlock. Here are some example ways:
79 - **Requirement**: For any loop / waiting, ensure it can break the deadlock. Clearly explain the initialization logic in the ‘protocol‘ field.
80 - **Examples**:
81 1. **Active Trigger**: "In a closed feedback loop (A↔B), configure Model A to send an initial ’start’ signal to Model B at T=0 to kick off the cycle."
82 2. **Pre-loaded Credit**: "Initialize the Manager with ‘credits=N‘, allowing it to dispatch N tasks immediately without waiting for the first ’worker_free’ signals."
83 3. **Early Registration**: "Configure Workers to send a ’register’ event to the Router at T=0, ensuring the Router has valid destinations populated before the first packet arrives."
84 - **Supreme Court Rule**: If [Parent Model Specification] implies a connection that creates a cold-start deadlock (unless explicitly desired), you MUST fix it by ensuring proper initialization.
85
86 {feedback}
87
88 ## [System Context]
89 This section describes the **EXISTING** environment around ‘{name}‘.
90 Use this to understand **WHO** connects to ‘{name}‘’s ports and **WHAT** kind of data flows there.
91 {context_str}
92
93 ## [Parent Model Specification]
94 (This is the model ‘{name}‘ you are splitting now)
95 {spec}

2 You are a DEVS Systems Architect. Analyze the requirements for model ‘{name}‘ and determine if it must be **Atomic** or **Coupled**.
3
4 **Utils Provided to DEVS Models**:
5 - Logger: we implemented a customized logger to collect log messages in a standard way.
6 - get_current_time: we implemented a function to get the current simulation time.
7
8 ## [Requirements]
9 {req}
10
11 ## [System Context]
12 This section describes the **EXISTING** environment around ‘{name}‘.
13 {context_str}
14
15 ## [Criteria]
16 - You should only consider the function described to decide if the model is atomic or coupled. You should not consider the complexity of logging and error handler requirements.
17 - The requirement does not state all the sub-model details, so it is allowed to add unmentioned components if necessary.
18 - **Atomic Model Criteria (Must meet ALL to be Atomic):**
19 - **Indivisibility:** The logic represents a single, basic action, and could not be divided (e.g., Generator, Queue, Router, Delay).
20 - **Single Responsibility:** It manages ONE simple state lifecycle. (e.g. Idle -> Active -> (Other) -> Done)
21 - **No Internal Flow:** It does not describe a pipeline of distinct steps.
22 - **Simple Logic:** The state transition logic requires a small set of variables to track progress.
23 - **Coupled Model Criteria (If ANY are true, it MUST be Coupled):**
24 - **Internal Workflow:** The requirement describes a process with multiple distinct stages (e.g., a "Server" that has an internal "buffer" AND a "processing unit").
25 - **Component Composition:** The description implies the existence of multiple meaningful sub-components.
26 - **Complex Logic:** If the state transition logic requires a massive set of variables to track progress.
27 - **God Object:** If the model handles input, processing, AND storage logic simultaneously.
28 - **Not Sure:** If you are not sure about the model type, you can choose this option and provide your reasoning.
29
30 - *Special*: Please distinguish between ‘A complex model containing multiple departments‘ and ‘A department coordinator‘. The former is coupled, the latter is atomic (if the router logic is not complex). Distinguish them based on the ports: coordinator must itself have ports to interact with siblings it coordinates.
31
32 ## [Instruction]
33 - If you choose **Coupled**, you MUST list the possible ‘submodels‘ you identified in the JSON output.
34 - If you choose **Atomic**, ‘submodels‘ should be empty.

1 ## [Global Standards]
2 Adhere to the following engineering standards for all model types:
3
4 ### 1. Imports \& Dependencies
5 - **Whitelist**: Restrict imports to the following packages: ‘numpy‘, ‘math‘, ‘random‘, ‘time‘, ‘pandas‘, ‘xdevs‘ (and ‘xdevs.models‘).
6 - **Project Utils**: Import necessary utilities (e.g., ‘get_sim_logger‘, ‘get_current_time‘) from ‘devs_project.devs_utils.xxx‘. Refer to [Utils] for detailed import statements.
7 - Other submodels in the project can be imported as needed.
8
9 ### 2. Data Protocol \& Typing
10 - You are only allowed to use the following Atomic Primitives and Composite Types in ports and arguments.
11 - **Atomic Primitives**: Only ‘int‘, ‘float‘, ‘str‘, ‘bool‘ instances for all base values.
12 - **Composite Types**: Only ‘dict‘ and ‘list‘.
13 - **Consistency**: Ensure that all ports and arguments are the same as those stated in the [Specification].
14 - **Recursive Schema Definition**:
15 - Recursively define the structure of all composite arguments (in ‘__init__‘) and port data types (in Docstrings).
16 - Continue the definition until all fields resolve to Atomic Primitives.
17 - **Dictionaries**: Explicitly list every Key name, the Type of its Value, and the explanation of it.
18 - **Lists**: Explicitly state the Type of elements contained in the list.
19 - Special: only the ‘parent‘ argument of the ‘__init__‘ method can be of type ‘Coupled | None‘.
20
21 ### 3. Type Docstring Schema
22 - **Structure**: Follow this hierarchy for describing types in Class and Method docstrings:
23 - Root: ‘name (type): Description‘
24 - Dict Keys: Indent 2-4 spaces, ‘key_name (type): Description‘
25 - List Items: Indent 2-4 spaces, ‘- (type): Description‘
26 - *Exception*: For Logging, you can refer to the structure described in the ports section, as they are often the same.
27 - **Example**:
28 ‘‘‘python
29 \"\"\"
30 ...
31 - in_packet (dict): Network packet.
32 header (dict): Protocol header.
33 src_ip (str): Source IP.
34 payload (str): Data content.
35 - batch_updates (list[dict]): Updates.
36 - (dict): Single update.
37 node_id (int): Target ID.
38 \"\"\"
39 ‘‘‘
40
41 ### 4. Coding Conventions
42 - **Explicit Configuration**: Define all configuration parameters explicitly in ‘__init__‘. Omit ‘*args‘ and ‘**kwargs‘.
43 - **Logging**: Log all key events using ‘self.logger.info({{"key": "value"}}, log_type=...)‘. The main msg must be a dict. They must have the exact precise structure and keys as the context (especially the system goal) and the Model Specification. You should explain the structure of the data in the docstring. However, you only need to list the logging happen in this model, those in submodels are strictly forbiddened.
44 - **Parameter Storage**: Store internal hardcoded parameters (not passed via ‘__init__‘) in a ‘self.param‘ dictionary.
⬇
1 ### [Atomic Model Specifics]
2 0. Must import: ‘from xdevs.models import Atomic, Coupled, Port‘. Atomic for inherit, Coupled for __init__ arg type.
3 1. **Inheritance**: Inherit from ‘Atomic‘.
4 2. **Docstring**: The class MUST include a standard class docstring strictly following this format:
5 ‘‘‘python
6 class {name}(Atomic):
7 \"\"\"
8 Function:
9 - ...General function
10 - ...Every state: how it transfer, and what to output after the state is over.
11 Logging in this model:
12 - ...
13 - ...
14 Input Ports:
15 - port_name (type): description
16 structure: ...
17 protocol: initialize: ... ; process: ...
18 Output Ports:
19 - port_name (type): description
20 structure: ...
21 protocol: initialize: ... ; process: ...
22 \"\"\"
23 ‘‘‘
24 3. **Constructor (‘__init__‘)**:
25 - Signature: ‘def __init__(self, name: str, parent: Coupled | None, <explicit_config_args>)‘
26 - Docstring: should have a docstring describing the arguments, including the detailed type and description. using the following format:
27 ‘‘‘python
28 \"\"\"
29 Args:
30 name (str): The unique name of the model.
31 parent (Coupled | None): the parent model. If None, the model is a root model.
32 arg_name1 (type): description
33 \"\"\"
34 ‘‘‘
35 - Steps:
36 1. Call ‘super().__init__(name)‘.
37 2. Assign ‘self.parent = parent‘.
38 3. Initialize logger: ‘self.logger = get_sim_logger(self)‘.
39 4. Register Ports: Use ‘self.add_in_port(Port(type, "name"))‘ and ‘self.add_out_port(Port(type, "name"))‘.
40 5. Initialize State: Set member variables and call ‘self.hold_in(phase, time)‘.
41 6. Log creation: ‘self.logger.info({{keys: values, ...}}, log_type=...)‘
42 4. **Core Behaviors**:
43 - Implement ‘initialize(self)‘: Set initial state. Set phase/sigma using ‘self.hold_in(phase, time)‘. Log initialization.
44 - It can not send any output. If you need to send a initial signal (e.g. report you are ready), you can use ‘self.hold_in(phase, time)‘ to schedule the event, prepare the payload, and send it in ‘lambdaf‘.
45 - If any port has ‘initial_signal‘ to emit immediately or after a duration, the ‘initialize‘ method **MUST** schedule an output event using ‘self.hold_in("SOME_STATE", duration)‘.
46 - Implement ‘lambdaf(self)‘: Only do the output, any other operations should be done in the following ‘deltint‘:
47 - Send output via ‘self.output["port"].add(payload)‘.
48 - DO NOT change the state, sigma, kpi_counter, etc. Leave that to the following ‘deltint‘.
49 - Implement ‘deltint(self)‘: Only do the following:
50 - Get the old internal state: ‘self.phase‘. Get total time(from last state change to expected next state change, which is just the sigma set last time): ‘self.ta()‘.
51 - Handle internal timeouts. And update the internal queue / kpi_counter / etc. accordingly. (Because deltint is called right after lambdaf, which means the output of the old state is already sent).
52 - Prepare the payload of the output of the next phase. Make sure the prepared payload is the one used in ‘lambdaf‘ of the new phase.
53 - Always schedule next internal event in the end: ‘self.hold_in(phase, sigma)‘. If not interrupted, the model will emit the output prepared after sigma time units.
54 - Log events (if needed).
55 - Implement ‘deltext(self, e)‘: Only do the following:
56 - Handle external events (‘self.input["port"].values‘).
57 - Get internal state: ‘self.phase‘. Get total time(from last state change to expected next state change, which is just the sigma set last time): ‘self.ta()‘.
58 - Prepare the payload of the next lambdaf. Make sure the prepared payload variable is the one used in ‘lambdaf‘.
59 - Always schedule next internal event in the end: ‘self.hold_in(phase, sigma)‘.
60 - Log events (if needed).
61 - Implement ‘exit(self)‘: Cleanup and final stats logging.
62 - **Event Handling Logic**:
63 - **Execution Sequence (CRITICAL)**: ‘lambdaf‘ will send outputs before ‘deltint‘ schedules the next internal event. Thus, the payload sent in ‘lambdaf‘ should be prepared in the previous ‘deltint‘, ‘deltext‘, or ‘initialize‘.
64 - **Confluent Events (‘deltcon‘)**: By default, internal events (‘deltint‘) take precedence over external events when they occur simultaneously. Explicitly override the ‘deltcon(self)‘ method ONLY IF you need to change this logic (e.g., to process external events first).
65 - **Initialization**: Realize the ports.protocol’s initialize descriptions:
66 - initial_signal: If a signal or information should be sent at initialization(i.e. protocol.initial_signal), you can use ‘self.hold_in("INIT", 0)‘ to schedule the event and send it in ‘lambdaf‘. This is the only way to send a signal at initialization.
67 - initial_state: modify the logic and initial values to make sure it is realized.
68 5. **logging requirements**: make sure all the events required are logged. And the keys and structures of the logs must match the Specification exactly.
